questions.q: What are the two real entry points for writing and running Q# today?
options: A standalone .qs project run via the VS Code QDK extension's Run code lens, or Q# written inside Python/Jupyter via the `qsharp` package
A web-only browser IDE, or a command-line-only compiler with no editor support
The legacy standalone IQ# Jupyter kernel, or a Visual Studio (not VS Code) plugin
Azure Portal's built-in code editor, or a mobile app
questions.explain: Today's QDK supports a standalone .qs project driven by the VS Code extension's Run/Debug code lens, and a Python/Jupyter workflow via the `qsharp` package -- both compile the same Q# language through different harnesses.

questions.q: What is the modern, current way to use Q# inside a Jupyter notebook?
options: Install the `qsharp` (and optionally `qsharp-widgets`) Python package and use `%%qsharp` cells or `qsharp.run(...)`, not the older standalone IQ# kernel
Install a separate IQ# Jupyter kernel, which remains the only supported notebook method
Jupyter cannot run Q# under any circumstances
Convert all Q# code to Qiskit syntax first, then run it as Python
questions.explain: The old standalone IQ# Jupyter kernel has been superseded by the `qsharp` Python package, which lets you write Q# directly in `%%qsharp` notebook cells or pass source to `qsharp.run`/`qsharp.eval` from Python.

questions.q: What does the presence of a `qsharp.json` file at a folder's root signal to the QDK tooling?
options: That the folder is a Q# project root, which enables correct multi-file compilation and project-aware tooling
That the folder contains only Python code, not Q#
That the project has already been submitted to Azure Quantum hardware
That the folder's `.qs` files should be ignored by the compiler
questions.explain: `qsharp.json` is the manifest that marks a directory as a Q# project root, which is what lets the VS Code extension and compiler treat files under `src/` as part of one coherent project.

questions.q: What attribute does the QDK look for to know which operation starts a standalone Q# program, and where does it typically appear?
options: `@EntryPoint()`, placed directly above the operation that should run first, commonly in `src/Main.qs`
`@Main`, placed at the top of the `qsharp.json` manifest file
`#!/usr/bin/qsharp`, as the first line of the file
No attribute is needed -- the compiler always runs the first operation defined in the file
questions.explain: `@EntryPoint()` marks the operation where execution begins; it's what the VS Code Run/Debug code lens and the compiler use to find the program's starting point, conventionally in a file like src/Main.qs.

questions.q: At the setup stage described in this lesson, does running a Q# program on the local simulator require an Azure account or Azure Quantum workspace?
options: No -- local simulation runs entirely on your own machine with no Azure account, subscription, or workspace involved
Yes -- every Q# program, even on the local simulator, must first authenticate against an Azure Quantum workspace
Only if you use the VS Code extension; the Python package never needs local simulation
Only if your program allocates more than one qubit
questions.explain: Local simulation via either entry point (VS Code Run lens or the Python `qsharp` package) runs on your own machine against the built-in simulator; an Azure Quantum workspace only becomes necessary later, for resource estimation or real hardware submission.
